text:
Does this work for a qualified covered call?

Imagine an investor has owned the XYZ company  (not a real company) for a long time with a low cost basis. He then writes an out of the money qualified call option against it.

The stock continues to go up. He does not want to pay tax on the capital gain at this time. He could buy back the call at a loss but the loss would be a long term capital loss. He would like to generate a short term capital loss. As a result, he does the following. He buys additional shares of the XYZ stock and then sells them at a loss. That should generate a short term capital loss.

I was told that I am wrong. Here is a reason why I think I might be wrong. The sale of a covered call is still a straddle for tax purposes. As such, I am thinking (but I am not sure of that) at the time you sell the calls you have to identify which shares are part of the covered call. As a result, you can not later claim that the shares you sold were the ones you just bought.

However, I feel I am right because of section 1092(c) of the tax code. Section 1092(c) says that covered calls are normally given an exemption from section 1092. For details on section 1092 you can look here: 
Text of section 1092

You will observe that section 1092 says:
Section 1092(c)(4) provides an exception to the general rule that a straddle exists if a taxpayer holds stock and writes a call option on that stock. Under section 1092(c)(4), the ownership of stock and the issuance of a call option meeting certain requirements result in a qualified covered call, which is exempted from the general straddle rules of section 1092.

Therefore, I feel I am right. Am I?

text:
Why isn't the "erase and replace" strategy routine for avoiding estimated payments and delaying taxes (for married retirees with IRAs, at least)?

Assume that a retired, married U.S. couple receives capital gains, possibly erratic, throughout the year for whatever reason.

The prevailing recommendation is to complete IRS Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year* to calculate estimated tax payments and to make these payments in a timely manner to avoid penalties. The (sometimes needless**) payments represent money that's no longer available to earn income.

As an alternative, consider the "erase and replace" approach, in which withholding from an IRA rollover is used to satisfy the required payments. (
1
, 
2
, 
3
, 
4
.) (The IRS considers withholding at any point in the year to be distributed evenly over the four payment periods.) In this strategy, the couple makes zero estimated payments throughout the year and then performs an indirect IRA rollover each December in the amount of 90% of that year's tax or 100-110% of last year's tax (depending on their AGI), whichever is less. It's arranged that 100% of the rollover is withheld for federal taxes; the rollover is completed soon after with cash. An indirect rollover is permitted every 12 months per person; to avoid having the date creep forward when meeting this requirement, the couple alternates between rollovers for each person, resulting in ~24 months spacing.

Thus,

Federal tax is considered to be paid in a timely manner,

No penalties are incurred,

Form 2210 can potentially be ignored, and

Instead of making estimated payments (which may be refunded anyway, as described below), that money can be used to earn income starting as early as April 15 (the deadline for the first estimated payment) to the rollover replacement date (as @littleadv indicates, this minimizes the amount of time the rollover money is absent from the IRA).

Note that this strategy addresses federal tax only; state laws vary regarding withholding and estimated payments.

I see no indication that this approach is recommended for routine use, so either there's an error or it's an obscure edge case
 (although it doesn't seem unusual for a retired couple to both have IRAs and also receive capital gains). I appreciate your comments.

*Example of a "gotcha" if the couple doesn't complete Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year: The couple receives capital gains of $125K in January and then unexpected capital gains of $125K more in December. They spend most of the year paying zero estimated taxes, as their January income is tax free under the standard deduction and 0% capital gains bracket. Nonresident alien with U.S.-source §988 gain: ECI, FDAP, or not taxable?

Facts

•   Taxpayer is a nonresident alien who does not meet the substantial presence test but lives and works in the U.S.

•   After moving to the U.S. and establishing a U.S. tax home through employment, the taxpayer converts foreign personal savings (e.g., EUR) to USD.

•   The foreign currency represents personal savings accumulated over multiple prior years; upon conversion, the USD amount realized exceeds the taxpayer’s basis determined under §988 due solely to exchange-rate movements.

•   The resulting foreign currency gain is ordinary income under §988.

Sourcing

Under §865, foreign currency gain is sourced by the taxpayer’s residence, and residence is determined by tax home under §911(d)(3).
Because the taxpayer’s principal place of business is in the U.S., the §988 gain appears to be U.S.-source income.

Issue:
 How is this §988 gain taxed to a nonresident alien?

Analysis

•   The gain does not appear to be effectively connected income (ECI): it arises from personal savings and is not connected to a U.S. trade or business; the taxpayer’s U.S. employment is not a material factor in producing the gain.

•   The gain also does not appear to be FDAP income:

Under Reg. §1.988-3(c)(1), exchange gain or loss on a §988  transaction is not treated as interest, except in limited,

specifically enumerated cases (e.g., certain tax-exempt bonds, integrated debt hedges).

The §988 regulations treat the conversion of nonfunctional currency as a sale or other disposition of property, applying §1001 amount-realized and basis mechanics.

Gains from sales or other dispositions of property are excluded from FDAP under Reg. §1.1441-2(b)(2)(i).

Question

If the gain is U.S.-source but is neither ECI nor FDAP, is it correct that the §988 gain is not taxable to the nonresident alien under §871, notwithstanding its ordinary character?

This ignorant investor does not know that the price of the first stock minus the price of the second will never fluctuate and will always remain zero. Annual maintenance costs on the property are $1,500 per year and are not tax deductible. You expect property taxes and maintenance costs to increase at the rate of inflation. Your income tax rate is 40%, you can earn an after-tax real interest rate of 2% per year, and you plan to keep the apartment forever. What is the "breakeven" annual rent such that you would buy it if the rent exceeds this amount?

Solution
: $6,700 per year

My confusion stems from reading

you can earn an after-tax real interest rate of 2% per year

Does it mean that if you were to invest the $335,000 at a 2% rate you will earn $6,700 per year or would you rather pay $6,700 every year for the rest of your life by choosing to own the house?

Full solution
:

The after-tax annual outlay from the purchase is:
1500 + (100%−40%) ∗2000 = $2, 700

The present value of this perpetuity is: 2700/2% = $135, 000

The present value of the costs of owning are:
135000 + 200000 = $335, 000

The break-even rent is: 2% ∗335000 = $6, 700 per year.

Two US taxpayers, A and B, own a home together as joint tenants.  They both live in the home, and it is their "main home" for tax purposes.  A and B are not married to each other and never have been, and they each file their taxes as "single".

home mortgage interest deduction
.  They each pay half of the monthly mortgage payments.  Must they divide the deduction equally, or may they divide it unequally if this is advantageous to them?

For example, suppose that in a given year, the mortgage payments totaled $40,000, of which $10,000 was principal and $30,000 was interest.  A and B each paid $20,000.

By default, each of them would say they paid $5,000 in principal and $15,000 in interest, and each would take a $15,000 mortgage interest deduction. Pub. 936 (linked above) has a section "More than one borrower":

More than one borrower.
 If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on a mortgage that was for your home, and the other person received a Form 1098 showing the interest that was paid during the year, attach a statement to your paper return explaining this. Show how much of the interest each of you paid, and give the name and address of the person who received the form. Deduct your share of the interest on Schedule A (Form 1040), line 8b, and print “See attached” next to the line.

But it does not specify how the shares are to be determined.
